claim: TRAAK is a membrane tension-activated K+ channel.
source: TRAAK is a membrane tension-activated K+ channel that has been associated through behavioral studies to mechanical nociception.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a defining characteristic of TRAAK.

claim: TRAAK has been associated through behavioral studies to mechanical nociception.
source: TRAAK is a membrane tension-activated K+ channel that has been associated through behavioral studies to mechanical nociception.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior behavioral studies.

claim: TRAAK is localized exclusively to nodes of Ranvier in mice.
source: We used specific monoclonal antibodies in mice to show that TRAAK is localized exclusively to nodes of Ranvier, the action potential propagating elements of myelinated nerve fibers.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunostaining data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Approximately 80 percent of myelinated nerve fibers throughout the central and peripheral nervous system contain TRAAK.
source: Approximately 80 percent of myelinated nerve fibers throughout the central and peripheral nervous system contain TRAAK in what is likely an all-nodes or no-nodes per axon fashion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantification data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: TRAAK is present in an all-nodes or no-nodes per axon fashion.
source: Approximately 80 percent of myelinated nerve fibers throughout the central and peripheral nervous system contain TRAAK in what is likely an all-nodes or no-nodes per axon fashion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by teased fiber experiments in Figure 4.

claim: TRAAK is not observed at the axon initial segment where action potentials are first generated.
source: TRAAK is not observed at the axon initial segment where action potentials are first generated.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: TRAAK contributes to the 'leak' K+ current in mammalian nerve fiber conduction by hyperpolarizing the resting membrane potential.
source: TRAAK contributes to the 'leak' K+ current in mammalian nerve fiber conduction by hyperpolarizing the resting membrane potential, thereby increasing Na+ channel availability for action potential propagation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological recordings in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: TRAAK hyperpolarizes the resting membrane potential, thereby increasing Na+ channel availability for action potential propagation.
source: TRAAK contributes to the 'leak' K+ current in mammalian nerve fiber conduction by hyperpolarizing the resting membrane potential, thereby increasing Na+ channel availability for action potential propagation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by RU2 experiments in Figure 7.

claim: Mechanosensitive channels are cells' fastest force sensors.
source: Force-gated or mechanosensitive ion channels are cells' fastest force sensors and are gated open by mechanical force to transduce physical stimuli into cellular electrical signals (Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Mechanosensitive ion channels are gated open by mechanical force to transduce physical stimuli into cellular electrical signals.
source: Force-gated or mechanosensitive ion channels are cells' fastest force sensors and are gated open by mechanical force to transduce physical stimuli into cellular electrical signals (Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Mechanosensitive channels were first implicated in auditory transduction three decades ago.
source: First implicated in auditory transduction three decades ago (Corey and Hudspeth, 1979), mechanosensitive channels are best known for their roles in the classic senses of touch and hearing.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Corey and Hudspeth, 1979.

claim: Mechanosensitive channels are best known for their roles in the classic senses of touch and hearing.
source: First implicated in auditory transduction three decades ago (Corey and Hudspeth, 1979), mechanosensitive channels are best known for their roles in the classic senses of touch and hearing.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Mechanosensitive ion channels underlie proprioception, blood pressure regulation and osmolarity control.
source: However, mechanosensitive ion channels also underlie less conspicuous force sensations such as proprioception, blood pressure regulation and osmolarity control (Teng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Nearly all cell types express mechanosensitive channels including stem cells, cancer cells and neurons of the central nervous system.
source: The prevalence of mechanically-activated currents in cells has become increasingly clear; nearly all cell types express mechanosensitive channels including stem cells, cancer cells and neurons of the central nervous system, suggesting, perhaps, that force sensation by ion channels may be involved in more aspects of physiology than previously appreciated (Ranade et al., 2015; Teng et al., 2015; Anishkin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: TRAAK is a mechanosensitive ion channel from the two-pore domain K+-selective (K2P) channel family.
source: TRAAK (TWIK-related arachidonic acid activated K+ channel) is a mechanosensitive ion channel from the two-pore domain K+-selective (K2P) channel family (Fink et al., 1998; Maingret et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: K2P channels give rise to what have traditionally been called 'leak currents' because they approximate the voltage- and time-independent properties of a simple K+-selective hole in the membrane.
source: K2P channels give rise to what have traditionally been called 'leak currents' because they approximate the voltage- and time-independent properties of a simple K+-selective hole in the membrane (Enyedi and Czirják, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: The activity of K2Ps can be diversely regulated to control cellular excitability.
source: However, it is now appreciated that the activity of K2Ps can be diversely regulated to control cellular excitability (Renigunta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: TRAAK is gated open by force directly through the lipid bilayer.
source: TRAAK is gated open by force directly through the lipid bilayer (Brohawn et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to prior work.

claim: In the absence of tension, TRAAK displays low activity with an open probability estimated to be less than 1%.
source: In the absence of tension, TRAAK displays low activity with an open probability estimated to be less than 1% (Brohawn et al., 2014b; Kang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: TRAAK is rapidly and increasingly activated from very small applied forces up to the lytic tension of the membrane.
source: The channel is rapidly and increasingly activated from very small applied forces up to the lytic tension of the membrane (Brohawn et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Activation of TRAAK involves protein conformational changes that prevent membrane lipids from entering the conduction pathway and blocking K+ passage.
source: Activation of TRAAK involves protein conformational changes that prevent membrane lipids from entering the conduction pathway and blocking K+ passage.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on structural work.

claim: TRAAK changes shape upon opening, expanding and becoming less conical and more cylindrical in the plane of the membrane.
source: TRAAK changes shape upon opening, expanding and becoming less conical and more cylindrical in the plane of the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on structural studies.

claim: TRAAK shape changes are energetically favored when lateral tension is applied.
source: These shape changes are energetically favored when lateral tension is applied.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the mechanistic model.

claim: TRAAK is reported to be broadly expressed in neurons of the central and peripheral nervous system.
source: TRAAK is reported to be broadly expressed in neurons of the central and peripheral nervous system, but the resolution of these studies is limited as they investigate the presence of TRAAK transcripts and they differ in detail (Fink et al., 1998; Talley et al., 2001; Lein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior transcript studies.

claim: TRAAK-/- mice display mechanical and temperature allodynia and enhanced mechanical hyperalgesia during inflammation.
source: TRAAK-/- mice display mechanical and temperature allodynia and enhanced mechanical hyperalgesia during inflammation, consistent with a role for TRAAK in thermal and mechanical nociception (Noël et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in TRAAK identified in three human families are thought to underlie a complex developmental and neurological disorder FHEIG.
source: Gain-of-function mutations in TRAAK identified in three human families are thought to underlie a complex developmental and neurological disorder FHEIG, an acronym for its characteristic phenotypes of facial dysmorphism, hypertrichosis, epilepsy, intellectual disability, and gingival outgrowth (Bauer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Nodes of Ranvier are the periodic ~1 μm gaps in myelination where the action potential is regenerated.
source: Nodes of Ranvier are the periodic ~1 μm gaps in myelination where the action potential is regenerated.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about nodes of Ranvier.

claim: Nodal membranes contain a high density of voltage-gated Na+ channels (Nav1.6), adhesion molecules, and scaffolding components including ankyrin G (AnkG).
source: Nodal membranes contain a high density of voltage-gated Na+ channels (Nav1.6), adhesion molecules, and scaffolding components including ankyrin G (AnkG).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge with citations.

claim: KV7.2/KV7.3 (KCNQ2/3) channels are incorporated into the nodal membrane.
source: In addition, KV7.2/KV7.3 (KCNQ2/3) channels are incorporated into the nodal membrane (Schwarz et al., 2006; Devaux et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Paranodes are tight cell-cell junctions between axonal and glial membranes made in part by Contactin-associated protein 1 (Caspr1).
source: Flanking the node are paranodes, tight cell-cell junctions between axonal and glial membranes made in part by Contactin-associated protein 1 (Caspr1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Juxtaparanodes contain voltage-gated K+ channels (Kv1.1 and Kv1.2).
source: Flanking the paranodes are juxtaparanodes, which contain voltage-gated K+ channels (Kv1.1 and Kv1.2) (Schwarz et al., 2006; Hille, 1967; Stämpfli and Hille, 1976; Chiu et al., 1979; Röper and Schwarz, 1989; Chiu and Ritchie, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: It has been known for about forty years that the K+ conductance in mammalian nodes is predominantly composed of leak-type rather than voltage-gated channels.
source: While it has been known for about forty years that the K+ conductance in mammalian nodes is predominantly composed of leak-type rather than voltage-gated channels (Chiu et al., 1979; Röper and Schwarz, 1989; Chiu and Ritchie, 1981; Brismar and Schwarz, 1985), TRAAK is, to our knowledge, the first molecularly identified component of this conductance.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: TRAAK is the first molecularly identified component of the leak K+ conductance in mammalian nodes of Ranvier.
source: While it has been known for about forty years that the K+ conductance in mammalian nodes is predominantly composed of leak-type rather than voltage-gated channels (Chiu et al., 1979; Röper and Schwarz, 1989; Chiu and Ritchie, 1981; Brismar and Schwarz, 1985), TRAAK is, to our knowledge, the first molecularly identified component of this conductance.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the manuscript stated in the introduction.

claim: The basal activity of TRAAK is involved in maintaining a negative nodal resting potential to increase nodal NaV channel availability.
source: We demonstrate that the basal activity of TRAAK is involved in maintaining a negative nodal resting potential to increase nodal NaV channel availability.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments in Figure 7.

claim: The anti-TRAAK monoclonal antibody recognizes an extracellular epitope.
source: The anti-TRAAK antibody labels live cells expressing TRAAK indicative of extracellular epitope recognition.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A where live cells are labeled.

claim: The anti-TRAAK antibody specifically labels mouse TRAAK and not related mouse K2P channels.
source: Candidate monoclonal antibodies were screened to identify one that met the following criteria: (i) it was biochemically well behaved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), (ii) it formed a tight complex with TRAAK (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), (iii) it recognized an extracellular epitope (Figure 1A), and (iv) it specifically labeled mouse TRAAK and not related mouse K2P channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The antibody binding site spans both subunits of the dimeric TRAAK channel.
source: The antibody binding site spans both subunits of the dimeric channel, with cap helix 1 of one protomer forming ~2/3 of the surface and cap helix two from the second protomer forming the remaining ~1/3.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the crystal structure.

claim: Most of the twenty epitope-forming residues are poorly conserved among K2P channels.
source: Most of the twenty epitope-forming residues are poorly conserved among K2P channels (Figure 1D), offering a molecular explanation for the high specificity of the antibody for TRAAK among all mouse K2Ps.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TRAAK is not present in lanceolate endings surrounding hair follicles.
source: However, we found no evidence for channel localization in sensory structures including lanceolate endings surrounding hair follicles and Merkel cells within touch domes of glabrous skin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TRAAK is not present in Merkel cells within touch domes of glabrous skin.
source: However, we found no evidence for channel localization in sensory structures including lanceolate endings surrounding hair follicles and Merkel cells within touch domes of glabrous skin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TRAAK-labeling was restricted to ~1 um3 puncta throughout the nervous system.
source: Instead, TRAAK-labeling was restricted to ~1 um3 puncta throughout the nervous system (e.g. Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TRAAK staining sites are not synapses.
source: These sites are not synapses as TRAAK staining is spatially distinct from PSD95-labeled terminals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TRAAK expression is neuronally restricted.
source: Consistent with previous reports of neuronally restricted TRAAK expression (Fink et al., 1998), antibody staining was distinct from astrocytic (GFAP-positive) and microglial (IBA1-positive) processes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: TRAAK is flanked by Caspr1, a hallmark constituent of paranodal regions flanking nodes of Ranvier.
source: Within neurons, TRAAK is flanked by Caspr1, a hallmark constituent of paranodal regions flanking nodes of Ranvier (Rasband and Shrager, 2000; Arroyo, 2004; Rasband and Peles, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations and shown in multiple figures.

claim: TRAAK co-localizes with known nodal components Nav1.6 and AnkG in sites delineated by flanking Caspr1 staining.
source: Co-staining with additional markers confirmed that TRAAK localized to nodes of Ranvier: TRAAK co-localizes with known nodal components Nav1.6 and AnkG in sites delineated by flanking Caspr1 staining (Figure 2B,D)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B,D.

claim: TRAAK, Caspr1, and Kv1.2 are present in three adjacent and non-overlapping domains corresponding to a central TRAAK-containing node, flanking Caspr1-containing paranodes, and Kv1.2-containing juxtaparanodes.
source: TRAAK, Caspr1, and Kv1.2 are present in three adjacent and non-overlapping domains (Figure 2C) corresponding to a central TRAAK-containing node, flanking Caspr1-containing paranodes, and Kv1.2-containing juxtaparanodes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C,E.

claim: TRAAK-labeling is absent from axon initial segments.
source: While co-localization of TRAAK and AnkG is observed in nodes of Ranvier, TRAAK-labeling is absent from initial segments.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: TRAAK appears to be restricted to the nodal compartment.
source: TRAAK appears to be restricted to the nodal compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the immunostaining data.

claim: TRAAK is found in nodes of Ranvier in optic nerve, spinal cord, and sciatic nerve.
source: TRAAK is found in nodes of Ranvier in optic nerve, spinal cord, and sciatic nerve co-localized with AnkG and flanked by paranodal Caspr1 and juxtaparanodal Kv1.2 (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: 73 ± 5% of nodes in the hippocampal-proximal fiber tracts of the fornix and fimbria contain TRAAK.
source: For example, 73 ± 5% of nodes in the hippocampal-proximal fiber tracts of the fornix and fimbria contain TRAAK (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: 79 ± 4% of nodes in the optic nerve are TRAAK-positive.
source: A similar percentage (79 ± 4%) of nodes in the optic nerve are TRAAK-positive (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: 16 ± 8% of nodes in fields of the ventral striatum and internal capsule were labeled with anti-TRAAK antibody.
source: 16 ± 8% of nodes in fields of the ventral striatum and internal capsule containing these tracts were labeled with anti-TRAAK antibody.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Motor neuron enriched ventral horns, sensory neuron enriched dorsal horns, and regions of the projected nerve containing a mixed population of motor and sensory fibers contain comparably high proportions of TRAAK-positive nodes (82 ± 4%, 86 ± 0.5% and 82 ± 0.2% respectively).
source: Motor neuron enriched ventral horns, sensory neuron enriched dorsal horns, and regions of the projected nerve containing a mixed population of motor and sensory fibers contain comparably high proportions of TRAAK-positive nodes (82 ± 4%, 86 ± 0.5% and 82 ± 0.2% respectively (mean ± standard deviation, n = 3)) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: 81 ± 2% of nodes in the spinal cord contained TRAAK.
source: 81 ± 2% of nodes in the spinal cord contained TRAAK (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: 82 ± 7% of nodes in the sciatic nerve are TRAAK-positive.
source: In the sciatic nerve, 82 ± 7% of nodes are TRAAK-positive (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: TRAAK is not specifically localized to either sensory or motor fibers.
source: We conclude that TRAAK is not specifically localized to either sensory or motor fibers and is present in a majority of nodes in the PNS.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the quantification data.

claim: All nodes within a fiber are either TRAAK-positive or TRAAK-negative.
source: We observe that all nodes within a fiber are either positive (axons 1–3) or negative (axons 4–5).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on teased fiber experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The occurrence of TRAAK in nodes is unlikely to be random.
source: The occurrence of TRAAK in nodes is therefore unlikely to be random.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on statistical analysis of teased fiber data.

claim: The data are consistent with there being two kinds of fibers, those with and those without TRAAK.
source: The data are more consistent with there being two kinds of fibers, those with and those without TRAAK.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the teased fiber experiments.

claim: In frog nodes, ~75% of the outward K+ current was blocked by TEA.
source: In frog nodes,~75% of the outward K+ current was blocked by TEA, whereas the remaining TEA-insensitive current is predominantly mediated by leak-type current (Hille, 1967; Stämpfli and Hille, 1976).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In rat nodes, the majority of the K+ current is TEA-insensitive and is largely composed of leak-type current.
source: In contrast, in rat nodes, the majority of the K+ current is TEA-insensitive and is largely composed of leak-type current (Chiu et al., 1979; Chiu and Ritchie, 1981; Brismar, 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the frog, TEA-sensitive KV channels are co-localized with NaV1.6 channels at the node.
source: In the frog, TEA-sensitive KV channels are co-localized with NaV1.6 channels at the node (Hille, 1967)
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation.

claim: In the rat, KV1 channels are restricted to the juxtaparanodal membrane and are absent in nodal axolemma uncovered by Schwann cell loops.
source: while in the rat, KV1 channels are restricted to the juxtaparanodal membrane and are absent in nodal axolemma uncovered by Schwann cell loops (Chiu et al., 1979; Röper and Schwarz, 1989; Brismar, 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations.

claim: Application of TEA depolarized the resting potential of frog nodes by ~4 mV.
source: Application of TEA depolarized the resting potential by ~4 mV, reduced the action potential amplitude by ~4 mV, prolonged the duration of the action potential by a factor of almost two, and typically abolished the afterhyperpolarization.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on recordings shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Application of TEA reduced the action potential amplitude of frog nodes by ~4 mV.
source: Application of TEA depolarized the resting potential by ~4 mV, reduced the action potential amplitude by ~4 mV, prolonged the duration of the action potential by a factor of almost two, and typically abolished the afterhyperpolarization.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on recordings shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Application of TEA prolonged the duration of the frog node action potential by a factor of almost two.
source: Application of TEA depolarized the resting potential by ~4 mV, reduced the action potential amplitude by ~4 mV, prolonged the duration of the action potential by a factor of almost two, and typically abolished the afterhyperpolarization.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on recordings shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Application of TEA typically abolished the afterhyperpolarization in frog nodes.
source: Application of TEA depolarized the resting potential by ~4 mV, reduced the action potential amplitude by ~4 mV, prolonged the duration of the action potential by a factor of almost two, and typically abolished the afterhyperpolarization.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on recordings shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Application of TEA depolarized the rat node resting potential by ~4 mV.
source: Application of TEA depolarized the rat node resting potential by ~4 mV and reduced the amplitude of the action potential by ~5 mV, but the duration of the action potentials remained almost unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Application of TEA reduced the amplitude of the rat node action potential by ~5 mV.
source: Application of TEA depolarized the rat node resting potential by ~4 mV and reduced the amplitude of the action potential by ~5 mV, but the duration of the action potentials remained almost unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The duration of rat node action potentials remained almost unchanged after TEA application.
source: Application of TEA depolarized the rat node resting potential by ~4 mV and reduced the amplitude of the action potential by ~5 mV, but the duration of the action potentials remained almost unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Repolarization of the frog action potential is brought about by a combination of NaV channel inactivation and delayed activation of TEA-sensitive KV channels.
source: Taken together, these data show that repolarization of the frog action potential is brought about by a combination of NaV channel inactivation and delayed activation of TEA-sensitive KV channels (Frankenhaeuser and Huxley, 1964)
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation.

claim: TEA-sensitive Kv channels do not play a significant role in repolarization of the action potential of the rat node of Ranvier.
source: In contrast, TEA-sensitive Kv channels do not play a significant role in repolarization of the action potential of the rat node of Ranvier (Chiu et al., 1979; Chiu and Ritchie, 1981; Brismar, 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations.

claim: In the mammalian node, K+-selective leak currents provide the K+ conductance necessary for node repolarization.
source: In the mammalian node, K+-selective leak currents provide the K+ conductance necessary for node repolarization and the time course of action potential repolarization is determined by that of Na+ channel inactivation (Schwarz et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation.

claim: The time course of action potential repolarization in mammalian nodes is determined by that of Na+ channel inactivation.
source: In the mammalian node, K+-selective leak currents provide the K+ conductance necessary for node repolarization and the time course of action potential repolarization is determined by that of Na+ channel inactivation (Schwarz et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation.

claim: Rat TRAAK is localized to nodes of Ranvier.
source: We generated a polyclonal antibody against mouse TRAAK that cross-reacts with the rat channel (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) and using this antibody, found that rat TRAAK is similarly localized to nodes of Ranvier (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: RU2 blocks rat TRAAK heterologously expressed in CHO cells.
source: We verified that RU2 also blocks rat TRAAK heterologously expressed in CHO cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In nodes of Ranvier recorded at 32-37°C, 10 or 20 µM RU2 blocked about 20% of the outward K+ current.
source: In nodes of Ranvier recorded at 32-37o C, 10 or 20 µM RU2 blocked about 20% of the outward K+ current (Figure 6A–D, n = 16 RU2-sensitive nodes).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: RU2-sensitive current was observed in 89% of rat nodes recorded at 32-37°C.
source: RU2-sensitive current was observed in 89% of rat nodes recorded at 32-37o C (Figure 6C, n = 18)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: RU2-sensitive current was observed in 86% of rat nodes recorded at either 32–37°C or room temperature.
source: or 86% of rat nodes recorded at either 32–37 o C or room temperature (n = 64 nodes).
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: RU2 application had no effect on 4 out of 4 frog nodes.
source: RU2 application had no effect on 4 out of 4 frog nodes.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: Application of RU2 depolarized the nodal membrane by ~4 mV.
source: Application of RU2 depolarized the nodal membrane by ~4 mV and resulted in a significant reduction in action potential amplitude (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Application of RU2 resulted in a significant reduction in action potential amplitude.
source: Application of RU2 depolarized the nodal membrane by ~4 mV and resulted in a significant reduction in action potential amplitude (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The reduction in action potential amplitude caused by RU2 was completely reversible upon washout.
source: This reduction was completely reversible upon washout.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In the presence of RU2, the amplitudes of repetitively elicited action potentials decrease until they reach a steady state level of diminished amplitude.
source: Repetitive 100 Hz stimulation exaggerates this effect: in the presence of RU2 the amplitudes of the repetitively elicited action potentials decrease until they reach a steady state level of diminished amplitude (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The RU2-induced reduction of the action potential amplitude is likely due to a depolarization-induced decrease in the number of NaV channels available for activation upon a depolarizing stimulus.
source: The RU2-induced reduction of the action potential amplitude is likely due to a depolarization-induced decrease in the number of NaV channels available for activation upon a depolarizing stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the NaV inactivation curve data.

claim: TRAAK-mediated leakage current is important for the stabilization of a negative resting potential and maximum spike amplitude.
source: These experiments demonstrate that TRAAK-mediated leakage current is important for the stabilization of a negative resting potential and maximum spike amplitude.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the RU2 experiments.

claim: TRAAK localization to nodes is not mediated through a direct interaction with AnkG.
source: This finding implies that unlike other nodal channels (including Navs and Kv3.1, 7.2, and 7.3 channels) (Rasband and Peles, 2015; Arancibia-Carcamo and Attwell, 2014), TRAAK localization to nodes is not mediated through a direct interaction with AnkG.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TRAAK is not present in axon initial segments despite AnkG being present there.

claim: TRAAK channels are only present in organisms that have myelinated axons and nodes of Ranvier – the gnathostomes or jawed vertebrates.
source: TRAAK channels are only present in organisms that have myelinated axons and nodes of Ranvier – the gnathostomes or jawed vertebrates for which evolution of axonal myelination with myelin basic protein is a defining characteristic (Nawaz et al., 2013; Nave and Werner, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: The contribution of TRAAK to nodal currents is not strictly conserved between species with TRAAK.
source: It is clear from the comparison of recordings from single rat and frog nodes presented here that the contribution of TRAAK to nodal currents is not strictly conserved between species with TRAAK.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: The basal activity of TRAAK plays a role in maintaining a negative resting potential, thereby increasing Nav channel availability and maximizing the action potential amplitude in rats.
source: The basal activity of TRAAK plays a role in maintaining a negative resting potential, thereby increasing Nav channel availability and maximizing the action potential amplitude in rats.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental results.

claim: Mammalian myelinated axons generally lack KV channel activity that could repolarize the membrane.
source: Indeed, mammalian myelinated axons generally lack KV channel activity that could repolarize the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge.

claim: The low open probability of TRAAK in resting membranes in the absence of mechanical force (<1% open) may be sufficient to support nodal repolarization.
source: The low open probability of TRAAK in resting membranes in the absence of mechanical force (<1% open) may be sufficient to support nodal repolarization.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation based on the known properties of TRAAK.

claim: K2Ps are capable (in simulations and culture cells) of supporting repolarization and repetitive spiking in the absence of Kv activity.
source: K2Ps are capable (in simulations and culture cells) of supporting repolarization and repetitive spiking in the absence of Kv activity (MacKenzie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.
